questions.question: What are the two main components installed when you install Docker?

explanation.correct: Docker installs two components: the Docker CLI (command-line interface where users type commands) and the Docker Daemon (background service that builds and runs containers).
explanation.why: Docker Desktop is a GUI tool for Mac/Windows. Docker Hub is an image registry, not a component of Docker itself.

questions.question: By default, which user can run Docker commands without sudo?

options.text: Any user in the sudoers file

explanation.correct: By default, only the root user can run Docker commands. Non-root users must be added to the docker group using: sudo usermod -aG docker username.
explanation.why: The Docker daemon runs as root, so by default only root can communicate with it. Adding a user to the docker group grants equivalent access.

questions.question: What is a Docker image?

options.text: A running instance of a container
A read-only template used to create containers
A backup of a running container

explanation.correct: A Docker image is a read-only template — a blueprint for creating containers. It contains the application code, dependencies, and configuration. A container is a running instance of an image.
explanation.why: A running instance is a container, not an image. An image is the static blueprint; the container is what's active and running.

questions.question: What command builds a Docker image from a Dockerfile?

explanation.correct: docker build -t myapp:v1 . builds an image from the Dockerfile in the current directory (.) and tags it as myapp:v1. The -t flag gives the image a name and optional tag.
explanation.why: docker run starts a container from an existing image. docker create and docker make are not valid commands for building images.

questions.question: What does the FROM instruction in a Dockerfile specify?

options.text: The base image to build upon
The command to run at startup

explanation.correct: FROM specifies the base image — a pre-built image from Docker Hub that your image builds upon. Example: FROM python:3.11-slim uses a lightweight Python image as the starting point.
explanation.why: EXPOSE sets ports, WORKDIR sets the working directory, CMD or ENTRYPOINT sets the startup command.

questions.question: What is Docker Hub?

options.text: The default public container image registry

explanation.correct: Docker Hub (hub.docker.com) is the default public container image registry. When you run docker pull ubuntu, Docker fetches the image from Docker Hub automatically.
explanation.why: Docker Hub stores and distributes container images, similar to how GitHub stores code. It's not a dashboard or networking tool.

questions.question: What AWS service is equivalent to Docker Hub but private and integrated with AWS?

explanation.correct: ECR (Elastic Container Registry) is AWS's private container image registry. It stores Docker images securely within your AWS account, integrated with IAM for access control.
explanation.why: S3 stores objects/files, ECS orchestrates containers, EBS is block storage. ECR is specifically for container images.

questions.question: What command shows all running Docker containers?

explanation.correct: docker ps shows all currently running containers. To see ALL containers including stopped ones, use docker ps -a.
explanation.why: docker images lists local images, not running containers. docker list and docker show are not valid Docker commands.

questions.question: What does Docker Compose do?

options.text: Compresses Docker images to save space
Manages multiple containers as a single application stack

explanation.correct: Docker Compose allows you to define multi-container applications in a single docker-compose.yml file. One command (docker-compose up) starts all defined services together.
explanation.why: Docker Compose is about orchestrating multiple containers. It uses a YAML file to configure services, networks, and volumes together.

questions.question: What is the default Docker network type for containers?

explanation.correct: Bridge is the default network type. All containers on the same host are automatically connected to the default bridge network, allowing them to communicate with each other.
explanation.why: Host network shares the host's network stack. Overlay spans multiple hosts. None provides no networking. Bridge is the standard default.

questions.question: Why do we use Docker Volumes?

options.text: To share Docker images between users
To persist data beyond the container lifecycle

explanation.correct: Docker volumes persist data outside the container. Without volumes, all data inside a container is lost when the container is deleted. Volumes store data on the host machine, surviving container restarts and deletions.
explanation.why: This is critical for databases — if your MongoDB container is deleted without a volume, all data disappears permanently.

questions.question: What does port mapping in Docker do?

options.text: Maps container names to IP addresses
Maps a host port to a container port for external access
Maps Docker commands to shell commands

explanation.correct: Port mapping (-p hostPort:containerPort) makes a container accessible from outside. For example, -p 8080:80 means traffic hitting the host on port 8080 gets forwarded to the container's port 80.
explanation.why: Without port mapping, containers are only accessible from within the Docker network. Port mapping opens them to the host and internet.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a limitation of using Docker alone in production?

options.text: No automatic container scaling on traffic spikes
No built-in load balancing across containers

explanation.correct: Docker can absolutely build images — that's one of its core features (docker build). The limitations of Docker alone are in production orchestration: no auto-scaling, no self-healing, no load balancing across multiple containers.
explanation.why: Building images is Docker's strength. The gaps are in managing containers at scale in production environments.

questions.question: What is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes?

explanation.correct: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. A Pod wraps one or more containers that share the same network namespace and storage. You don't run containers directly in Kubernetes — you run Pods.
explanation.why: Containers run inside Pods. Nodes are the machines that run Pods. Deployments manage multiple Pod replicas.

questions.question: What is the role of the Kubernetes API Server?

options.text: Act as the single entry point for all cluster communication

explanation.correct: The API Server (kube-apiserver) is the single control entry point — all requests from kubectl, other components, or external tools go through it. It validates, authenticates (RBAC), and routes requests.
explanation.why: etcd stores cluster state. The Scheduler places pods. Kubelet runs containers on nodes. The API Server is the communication hub.

questions.question: What does etcd store in a Kubernetes cluster?

options.text: The entire cluster state and configuration

explanation.correct: etcd is a distributed key-value store that holds the complete cluster state — which pods are running, their configurations, secrets, namespaces, and more. It's the cluster's source of truth and memory.
explanation.why: Images are stored in registries like ECR. Logs are stored in CloudWatch or similar. etcd is specifically for cluster state data.

questions.question: What is the function of the Kubernetes Scheduler?

options.text: Start and stop containers based on time
Decide which Worker Node a new Pod should run on
Monitor container health and restart failed ones
Handle incoming HTTP requests to the cluster

explanation.correct: The Scheduler is the decision engine for pod placement. When a new Pod is created, the Scheduler evaluates available Worker Nodes (CPU, memory, constraints) and decides which Node gets the Pod.
explanation.why: CronJob schedules time-based tasks. Controller Manager handles self-healing. Ingress/LoadBalancer handles HTTP traffic. The Scheduler focuses purely on pod placement decisions.

questions.question: What is 'self-healing' in Kubernetes?

options.text: Failed or crashed pods are automatically replaced without manual intervention
Docker images rebuild themselves when outdated

explanation.correct: Self-healing means Kubernetes continuously monitors Pod health and automatically recreates failed/crashed Pods to maintain the desired replica count. If you specify 3 replicas and one crashes, Kubernetes creates a replacement instantly.
explanation.why: Security patching is a separate process. Network healing and image rebuilding are not Kubernetes self-healing features.

questions.question: What is Kubelet in Kubernetes?

options.text: A CLI tool to manage Kubernetes clusters
An agent running on every Worker Node that bridges the Control Plane and container runtime
A load balancer for Kubernetes services
A type of Kubernetes storage volume

explanation.correct: Kubelet is an agent that runs on every Worker Node. It acts as the bridge between the Control Plane (which tells it what to run) and the local container runtime (which actually runs containers). It reports node status back to the Control Plane.
explanation.why: kubectl is the CLI tool. kube-proxy handles networking. PersistentVolume is storage. Kubelet is specifically the node agent.

questions.question: What is AWS ECS?

options.text: A serverless compute service for functions

explanation.correct: ECS (Elastic Container Service) is AWS's native container orchestration service. It manages Docker containers without requiring Kubernetes, deeply integrated with IAM, ALB, and CloudWatch.
explanation.why: ECR is the image registry. EKS is managed Kubernetes. Lambda is serverless functions. ECS is specifically AWS's own container orchestration.

questions.question: What is the ECS Task Definition?

options.text: A blueprint defining how a container should run in ECS

explanation.correct: A Task Definition is the blueprint for your container in ECS — it specifies the Docker image, CPU/memory requirements, port mappings, environment variables, and IAM roles. It's like a Dockerfile but for ECS.
explanation.why: A Task is the running instance. A Cluster is the grouping. IAM policies are separate security configurations.

questions.question: What is AWS Fargate?

options.text: A serverless compute engine for containers — no EC2 management required

explanation.correct: Fargate is a serverless compute engine for containers. You specify CPU/memory and provide your container image — AWS manages all underlying server infrastructure. No EC2 instances to provision or manage.
explanation.why: ECR handles images. EKS manages Kubernetes. Fargate eliminates the need to manage servers, making it truly serverless for containers.

questions.question: A company wants to run Kubernetes but doesn't want to manage the Control Plane. Which AWS service should they use?

explanation.correct: EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service) is AWS-managed Kubernetes. AWS manages and maintains the Control Plane (API server, etcd, controllers) for high availability. You only manage Worker Nodes and your workloads.
explanation.why: ECS is AWS-native, not Kubernetes. ECR stores images. Lambda is for functions. EKS is specifically managed Kubernetes on AWS.

questions.question: Which kubectl command deploys resources defined in a YAML file to a Kubernetes cluster?

explanation.correct: kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml creates or updates Kubernetes resources defined in the YAML file. 'apply' is preferred over 'create' because it's idempotent — running it again updates existing resources rather than erroring.
explanation.why: kubectl run starts a pod directly. kubectl create -f works but doesn't handle updates well. kubectl deploy is not a valid command.

questions.question: What is K8s an abbreviation for?

options.text: Kubernetes — K followed by 7 letters followed by s
Kubernetes — K followed by 8 letters followed by s

explanation.correct: K8s stands for Kubernetes where the '8' represents the 8 letters between 'K' and 's': u-b-e-r-n-e-t-e. Counting: K(ubernete)s = 8 letters in between.
explanation.why: This is a standard industry abbreviation called a numeronym. Similarly, i18n = internationalization (18 letters between i and n).

questions.question: In a Kubernetes cluster, what is the difference between the Control Plane and Worker Nodes?

options.text: Control Plane runs containers; Worker Nodes manage the cluster
Control Plane is the brain that makes decisions; Worker Nodes are where containers actually run
Control Plane handles networking; Worker Nodes handle storage
Control Plane is on-premises; Worker Nodes are in the cloud

explanation.correct: The Control Plane (API Server, etcd, Scheduler, Controller Manager) is the brain — it makes all decisions about scheduling, scaling, and healing. Worker Nodes are the execution layer where Pods and containers actually run.
explanation.why: The separation of concerns is fundamental to Kubernetes: control/decision-making happens in the Control Plane, execution happens in Worker Nodes.

questions.question: A startup wants to run containers on AWS without managing any servers. Traffic is variable. Which combination is most cost-effective?

explanation.correct: ECS with Fargate is ideal for a startup with variable traffic. Fargate eliminates server management (no EC2 to provision), and you pay only for the CPU/memory your containers use — scaling automatically with traffic.
explanation.why: Large EC2 instances are expensive and underutilized during low traffic. Spot instances are cheaper but can be interrupted. Docker Swarm requires more management than ECS.

questions.question: In Docker, what happens to data stored inside a container when the container is deleted?

options.text: Data is automatically backed up to S3
Data persists on the host machine
Data is saved to Docker Hub

explanation.correct: Containers are ephemeral — the writable layer inside a container is deleted when the container is removed. Without Docker volumes or bind mounts, all data inside the container is permanently lost.
explanation.why: This is why you must use volumes for any data that needs to persist — databases, logs, user uploads. The fix: docker run -v myvolume:/data/db mycontainer

questions.question: What Kubernetes feature automatically creates a new Pod replica when traffic increases?

explanation.correct: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) automatically scales the number of Pod replicas based on CPU/memory utilization or custom metrics. When traffic increases and CPU spikes, HPA creates additional replicas to handle load.
explanation.why: Self-healing replaces failed pods (same count). Rolling deployment handles updates. Kubelet is a node agent. HPA specifically handles scaling up/down based on demand.

questions.question: A team uses Kubernetes on AWS and needs to move workloads to Azure next year. Which approach preserves their investment?

options.text: Use ECS — AWS proprietary, so it's most optimized
Use EKS — Kubernetes skills and manifests are portable across clouds
Use Lambda — serverless avoids cloud lock-in

explanation.correct: Kubernetes is cloud-agnostic. EKS uses standard Kubernetes — the same kubectl commands, YAML manifests, and skills work on AKS (Azure), GKE (Google), or self-managed clusters. Moving to Azure means switching to AKS, not rewriting everything.
explanation.why: ECS is AWS-proprietary with no equivalent on other clouds. Lambda doesn't run container workloads the same way. Docker Swarm is less feature-rich and less adopted in production.
